claims.text: A controlled aging or thermomechanical treatment can induce nanoscale coherent intermetallic precipitates in an initially homogeneous refractory high-entropy alloy.
The intended precipitates would be analogous to gamma-double-prime strengthening precipitates.
The precipitates can be dispersed uniformly throughout the refractory HEA matrix.
Coherent intermetallic precipitates impede dislocation motion through precipitation strengthening.
Precipitation strengthening will increase the alloy's high-temperature yield strength.
Precipitation strengthening will improve the alloy's high-temperature creep resistance.
Controlling precipitate size and volume fraction can preserve room-temperature ductility.
The aging treatment and resulting precipitation will not adversely alter the alloy's density.
Mechanical capability at both room and elevated temperatures is relevant to aero-engine applications.
Temperatures from 700 to 1200 degrees Celsius under sustained tensile or creep loading are typical jet-turbine service conditions for the proposed alloy.
The improvement requires aging temperature and time to produce a high density of finely dispersed coherent precipitates.
Excessive precipitation or over-aging can cause precipitate coarsening or embrittlement.
Insufficient precipitate formation may fail to improve high-temperature properties.
The starting material is stipulated to be a homogeneous, single-phase refractory HEA without a deliberately introduced high-temperature strengthening precipitate.

Relative to an as-cast homogeneous baseline, the aged alloy is predicted to show a significant increase in high-temperature yield strength or creep resistance without degrading room-temperature properties or density.
